## Adding a Control Changed the Coefficient Last Week

Last week we added a control and the return to schooling changed. We could
say by how much, and we could say why.

::: {.tablenotes}
Two minutes with your neighbour. Every model we have written says one more
year of schooling is worth the same amount to everyone, at every level of
schooling. Where did we decide that? And would you defend it?
:::

## Lecture Plan

- **Logs and Elasticities.** Change the units and the coefficient answers a different question.
- **Dummy Variables.** A category shifts the intercept, relative to a base you chose.
- **Interactions.** Let the slope differ across groups, and every coefficient around it changes meaning.

::: {.tablenotes}
Reading: [to settle]. @huntingtonklein2022 is the accessible treatment of

# Logs and Elasticities

## The Straight Line Assumes Constant Returns to Schooling

**The goal of this section:** show that changing the units of a variable
changes the question its coefficient answers, and be exact about which
question.

Our model has said, without ever arguing for it, that the tenth year of
schooling and the twentieth year are worth the same 1.30 euro.

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The same 120 people twice: earnings
against schooling, and log earnings against schooling. Two straight lines,
two different claims about the world.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 3-2_levels-logs: two panels, same sample. Left, earnings on
     schooling with the fitted line. Right, log earnings on schooling with
     its fitted line. Needs identical point identities across panels so a
     student can follow one person from one panel to the other. -->

<!-- IDEA 1. 10-35 min. -->

## Logs Put the Change in Proportional Terms

**Objective:** ask what a year of schooling is worth as a proportion of what
a person already earns, rather than in euro.

$$\log(w_i) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 S_i + u_i$$

- $w_i$: hourly earnings of person $i$, in euro
- $\log(\cdot)$: the natural logarithm
- $S_i$: years of schooling
- $\beta_1$: the change in log earnings per year of schooling
- $u_i$: everything else

::: {.defn title="Semi-elasticity"}
$\beta_1$ is a semi-elasticity: an absolute change in $S$ mapped to a
proportional change in $w$. Multiply it by one hundred and you have a
percentage.
:::

## Four Specifications and What the Slope Means in Each

```{=latex}
\tabcaption{The same relationship under four specifications, and what the
slope answers in each.}

\begin{dgtable}{p{0.17\linewidth} p{0.20\linewidth} p{0.53\linewidth}}
\thead{Specification} & \thead{Regression} & \thead{What $\beta_1$ says} \\
\midrule
Level--level & $w$ on $S$ & One more year of schooling: $\beta_1$ euro
  more per hour. \\
Log--level   & $\log w$ on $S$ & One more year of schooling: about
  $100\beta_1$ percent more earnings. \\
Level--log   & $w$ on $\log S$ & One percent more schooling: about
  $\beta_1/100$ euro more per hour. \\
Log--log     & $\log w$ on $\log S$ & One percent more schooling: about
  $\beta_1$ percent more earnings. An elasticity. \\
\end{dgtable}

\dgnotes{Read the word ``about'' in the last three rows as a promise to come
back to it. Only the first row is exact.}
```

<!-- The table is the reference object for the rest of the section. Leave
     it up while the next two slides are discussed if the room allows. -->

## The Log-Log Slope Is a Unit-Free Elasticity

**Objective:** get a number that does not change when someone re-denominates
the data.

$$\log(w_i) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1 \log(S_i) + v_i$$

- $\gamma_1$: the elasticity of earnings with respect to schooling

::: {.result}
$\gamma_1$ is the percentage change in earnings for a one percent change in
schooling. Switch the data from euro to cents, or from years to months, and
$\gamma_1$ does not move. No other specification on that table can say that.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
The proof is two lines and it is in the appendix. Its shape: write the slope
as a derivative of logs, apply the chain rule twice, and the levels cancel.
The cancelling is the whole trick.
:::

## Percent and Percentage Point Are Not the Same Word

::: {.caveat title="The confusion that costs marks and papers"}
A **percentage change** is relative to where you started. A **percentage
point** is an absolute difference between two percentages. Earnings rising
from 10 to 11 euro is a ten percent rise. An employment rate going from 60
to 61 is a one percentage point rise, and a rise of about one and two thirds
percent.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
This is not a quibble about words. @schield2000 documents how badly students
at this stage describe and compare rates, and the ambiguity is in ordinary
English before it is in any regression. When your dependent variable is
itself a rate, the level-level coefficient is in percentage points and the
log-level coefficient is a percentage change of that rate. They are different
numbers and they answer different questions.
:::

## The Exact Percentage Change and When the Shortcut Fails

**Objective:** say exactly what a log-level coefficient implies, and then say
when the convenient version is good enough.

$$\%\Delta w = 100\left(e^{\beta_1} - 1\right)$$

::: {.worked title="How wrong is the shortcut?"}
- $\beta_1 = 0.05$: shortcut says 5, exact is 5.13
- $\beta_1 = 0.10$: shortcut says 10, exact is 10.52
- $\beta_1 = 0.20$: shortcut says 20, exact is 22.14
- $\beta_1 = 0.50$: shortcut says 50, exact is 64.87
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Below about 0.1 the shortcut is fine and everyone uses it. Above about 0.2
it is an error large enough to change a sentence in a results section, and it
is always in the same direction: the shortcut understates.
:::

## What Logs Cost: Zeros and an Imposed Shape

::: {.caveat}
You cannot take the log of zero, and in earnings data zero is not rare. The
usual fixes - add one, add a half, use $\log(1+w)$ - are choices about units
that change the answer, and @chen2024 shows the estimate can be made
arbitrarily large or small by the choice alone. We will not solve that in
this module. Know that it is a live problem and not a formality.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Second cost, and the one for this room: our population was generated as a
straight line in levels. A log specification fitted to it is a shape we
imposed. It will fit reasonably. It is still not what generated the data.
:::

## Vote: Percent or Percentage Point?

A regression of log earnings on a training dummy returns 0.08. A colleague
reports that training raises earnings by eight percentage points.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: what would the sentence
have to say instead, and what is the exact figure?
:::

# Dummy Variables

## A Category Enters the Model as an Intercept Shift

**The goal of this section:** put something that is not a number into a
regression, and know what the resulting coefficient is a comparison against.

**Objective:** allow two groups to sit at different levels while sharing a
slope.

$$w_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 S_i + \delta D_i + u_i$$

- $D_i$: one if person $i$ is in the group, zero otherwise
- $\delta$: the vertical gap between the two groups

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{Two parallel fitted lines through one
sample, split by a single dummy. The gap between them is the coefficient.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 3-2_dummy: one scatter, points coloured by the dummy, two
     parallel fitted lines. Needs the vertical gap annotated as delta, drawn
     at the sample mean of schooling rather than at zero. -->

<!-- IDEA 2. 38-63 min. -->

## The Coefficient Is a Difference Between Two Averages

::: {.result}
$\delta$ is the difference in average earnings between the two groups, at
the same level of schooling. With no other regressors it is exactly the
difference in the two group means.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
That is worth sitting with. A dummy in a regression with nothing else in it
is a comparison of two averages, which is the first thing anyone would have
done without regression at all. Regression earns its keep from the words
*at the same level of schooling*.
:::

## Dummy Coefficients Are Comparisons Against the Omitted Category

Four categories of highest qualification. You put in three dummies and the
software reports three numbers.

::: {.caveat title="The base you chose without noticing"}
Every one of those three numbers is a comparison against the category you
left out. You chose it. Very often R chose it for you, alphabetically. Change
the base and all three reported numbers change, while nothing about the world
does.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
In R the base is the first level of the factor, so `factor(qual)` orders
alphabetically unless you say otherwise. `relevel()` is one line and it is
the difference between a table that answers your question and a table that
answers an accident of spelling.
:::

## The Dummy Variable Trap: Why One Category Is Omitted

::: {.defn title="The dummy variable trap"}
Put in a dummy for every category as well as an intercept, and the four
dummies add up to the intercept exactly. There is no unique least squares
answer, because infinitely many sets of coefficients fit identically well.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
This is assumption four from week 6 failing, not a new problem. There is no
variation left in the last dummy once the other three and the intercept are
known. R will drop one silently and report the rest. Silently is the word to
worry about.
:::

## Dummy Coefficients When the Dependent Variable Is Logged

When earnings are logged, a dummy coefficient $\hat\delta$ is a proportional
gap, and the same approximation applies: about $100\hat\delta$ percent, and
exactly $100(e^{\hat\delta}-1)$ percent. @halvorsen1980 is the half-page note
that put this into applied practice, and @kennedy1981 refined the estimator
one step further.

::: {.tablenotes}
Two things worth saying about a pair of half-page notes from 1980. They are
cited thousands of times, which tells you how often the error was made. And
the correction still gets skipped, which tells you it is still being made.
:::

## Vote: What Is This Number Compared To?

A table reports coefficients on `apprenticeship`, `degree` and
`postgraduate`. Your co-author writes that the degree coefficient is the
return to a degree.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: what sentence would be
correct, and what else do you need to know before you can write it?
:::

# Interactions

## Interaction Terms Let the Slope Differ Across Groups

**The goal of this section:** allow the return to schooling to differ across
groups, and then be very careful about what every coefficient now means.

**Objective:** stop forcing one slope on two groups.

$$w_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 S_i + \delta D_i + \gamma (S_i \times D_i) + u_i$$

- $S_i \times D_i$: the product of the two, one variable, one column
- $\gamma$: the difference in slope between the groups

```{=latex}
\figsmall{../_shared/placeholder.pdf}{The same two groups, now with two
fitted lines that are not parallel. The difference in slope is the
interaction coefficient.}
```

<!-- FIGURE 3-2_interaction: same scatter and colours as 3-2_dummy so the
     two slides read as one argument. Two non-parallel fitted lines. Needs
     the slope difference annotated, and the two lines extended back to
     zero schooling in a lighter weight so the intercept gap is visible. -->

<!-- IDEA 3. 66-92 min. -->

## What the Schooling Coefficient Means After an Interaction

::: {.caveat title="Read this one carefully"}
Before the interaction, $\beta_1$ was the return to schooling. After it,
$\beta_1$ is the return to schooling **for the base group only**. It is not
an average, it is not the overall effect, and it did not stay what it was.
:::

- For the base group, the return is $\beta_1$.
- For the other group, the return is $\beta_1 + \gamma$.
- $\gamma$ answers whether the two differ, and by how much.

::: {.tablenotes}
This is the most common misreading in applied work and it is not a student
error. @brambor2006 read the published literature in an adjacent field and
found the majority of papers with interaction models interpreting these
coefficients wrongly, or omitting the terms needed to interpret them at all.
:::

## Why Centring Schooling Makes the Intercept Interpretable

With the interaction in, $\delta$ is the gap between the groups **at zero
years of schooling**. Nobody in our population has zero years of schooling.

::: {.result title="One line of R fixes it"}
Replace $S_i$ with $S_i - 12$. Every slope is unchanged. $\delta$ now
reports the gap at twelve years of schooling, which is a person who exists,
and the intercept reports expected earnings of 9.50 for the base group.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Centring is not a statistical repair. The fit is identical and the residuals
are identical. It relocates the point at which two of the coefficients are
reported, so that they are reported somewhere you can defend.
:::

## Testing the Slope Difference and Its Standard Error

The return for the other group is $\beta_1 + \gamma$, so its standard error
is not either standard error and not their sum. It needs the covariance
between the two estimates.

::: {.tablenotes}
Two honest routes. Refit with the other group as the base and read
$\beta_1 + \gamma$ straight off the output with its standard error attached.
Or test the two coefficients jointly, which is next week. Either way, note
that an interaction is estimated off the difference between two subgroup
slopes and is therefore much less precisely estimated than either.
:::

## Vote: Which Coefficient Answers the Question?

Log earnings on schooling, a dummy for women, and their interaction. You are
asked for the return to schooling for women.

::: {.tablenotes}
Vote, argue with your neighbour, vote again. Then: how would you report its
standard error?
:::

## What Would Have To Be True?

::: {.caveat title="The standing question"}
What would have to be true for this number to mean what we just said it means?
And what is the plausible story where it isn't?
:::

## Summary of Today's Three Functional-Form Choices

Today was three separate ideas, each doing one job:

::: {.contributions}
1. **Logs and Elasticities.** Logs change the question the coefficient answers, from euro to proportions, and the convenient percentage reading is an approximation with a known error.
2. **Dummy Variables.** A dummy shifts the intercept, and the number it reports is a comparison against a base category you chose.
3. **Interactions.** An interaction lets the slope differ, and the coefficient on the main term becomes the effect for the base group alone.
:::

::: {.tablenotes}
Next week: testing several coefficients at once, which is how you ask whether
a set of dummies or an interaction belongs in the model at all.
:::

## Derivation: Why a Log-Log Slope Is an Elasticity

Write the slope as a derivative of logs, apply the chain rule to each side,
and the levels cancel.

::: {.tablenotes}
Three steps. Differentiate $\log w$ with respect to $\log S$, write each as
a proportional change using the derivative of the logarithm, and take the
ratio. The step that does the work is the second: the derivative of $\log x$
is $1/x$, which is exactly what turns an absolute change into a proportional
one. The units cancel in the ratio, which is why an elasticity has none.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]

## Derivation: The Exact Percentage Change and the Shortcut Error

Start from the fitted model, difference it across a one-unit change in $S$,
exponentiate, and compare the exact result with the shortcut.

::: {.tablenotes}
Four steps. Write the fitted value at $S$ and at $S+1$, subtract, exponentiate
to get $e^{\beta_1}$ as the ratio of earnings, and subtract one for the
proportional change. The step that does the work is the last: the shortcut
replaces $e^{\beta_1}-1$ with $\beta_1$, which is the first term of its series
expansion. The error is of order $\beta_1^2/2$, which is why it is invisible
at 0.05 and embarrassing at 0.5.
:::

[Full derivation. Set as homework; worked solution published with the set.]

  a model with both main terms and their interaction.
- `I(x - 12)` inside a formula, which is centring without touching the data.
